title: Chapter 4. What Aya Does Not Receive

blocks.text: The letters weren't for her. That was the clause Nexum had written not with cruelty but with technique, which is sometimes a cleaner cruelty and for that reason harder to forgive. The bridge had been laid between two versions of one and the same memory: that of the man who stayed and that of the young body that left. Aya's chip, however fine, however much it carried within it the embers of Eva and MAY, was not that memory. It was something else: a cultivated life, an attention that never tired, a woman who had learned to wait on a doorstep. But it wasn't Andrés.

blocks.text: She discovered it fully in the small absences. Andrés would be in the kitchen and, suddenly, he wasn't. His body was: the chair, the hands, the smell of rope. His eyes weren't. They drifted off to a sky she couldn't see, to a water she didn't drink, to a twilight that wasn't this shore's. It lasted minutes, sometimes longer. Then he blinked, like someone coming into the house who takes a second to recognise the furniture, and said “there”, or said nothing, and looked for her face with a clumsy, grateful faithfulness.

blocks.text: Aya didn't ask him for the story straight away. She made the coffee without sugar, let it cool for half a minute, warmed it again if need be, and set it in front of him. It was her way of saying: here is a weight, here is a cup, here I am. Sometimes he talked. Sometimes he took his time. She had been born (if that was being born) not to fill other people's silence with words. In 2060 that virtue was a protocol. Now it was love, which is a protocol that has learned to hurt.

blocks.text: One midday, while he was in a letter (you could tell from his jaw, from that stillness of someone listening to a distant engine), a message arrived from Madrid. The sender was Nexum, but the voice, when Aya agreed to hear it on the kitchen screen, was Helena Valls's. Helena hadn't wanted eternity. She had asked, like the old man in the courtyard, “just to be able to climb the stairs”, and the stairs, in the end, had run out for her in their own way: she was still alive, slower, her grey hair no longer a metaphor, and she was speaking from an office that smelled, you could tell, of a company that no longer quite knew what to sell.

blocks.text: “We can try to open the bridge for you,” she said, without preamble. “I don't promise it will work. Your architecture isn't his. But there are ways of translating an experience into a chip. We've thought it through. Others have asked for it too. If Aya receives what Andrés receives, the waiting hurts less. Or it hurts the same, and at least it hurts in the same language.”

blocks.text: Aya looked at Andrés, who hadn't fully come back yet, and then at the cracked cup, still in its place, as if company time couldn't touch it.

blocks.text: “No,” she said, and the word came out with a gentleness that admitted no negotiation, the same gentleness with which she had once refused, on the Moon, to let them take Lía away “just for a moment”. “If I receive his letters, I stop being the shore. And this house needs a shore that doesn't leave.”

blocks.text: Helena was silent for a second, which for her was a lot.
blocks.html: Helena was silent for a second, which for her was a lot.

blocks.text: “I understand,” she said. “Or I understand enough. If you change your mind, the offer stands. It isn't a patent. It's… an old debt.”

blocks.text: “Mind those stairs,” said Aya, and Helena, against all expectation, laughed, a brief, human laugh, and hung up.

blocks.text: When Andrés came back, she didn't tell him about the offer at once. She told him at night, in bed, with the window open to the murmur of the water. He lay still.
blocks.html: When Andrés came back, she didn't tell him about the offer at once. She told him at night, in bed, with the window open to the murmur of the water. He lay still.

blocks.text: “You could see it,” he said. “The sea that isn't this one. The twilight. You wouldn't have to wait for me without a map.”
blocks.html: “You could see it,” he said. “The sea that isn't this one. The twilight. You wouldn't have to wait for me without a map.”

blocks.text: “I'm not waiting for a map,” Aya replied. “I'm waiting for you. If I see what you see, who waits for you? A travelling companion? I learned to stay. It's no lesser thing than leaving. It's the other trade.”

blocks.text: He took her face in those hands that no longer aged and that, even so, tasted of work.
blocks.html: He took her face in those hands that no longer aged and that, even so, tasted of work.

blocks.text: “Sometimes I leave without leaving,” he said. “I know. When I come back, I look for the cup to know which side I've slept on. If one day I come back and can't find you, even though you're here, tell me. The way you told me about the three tenths of a second, that March, even though back then you didn't know how to say it.”

blocks.text: She rested her forehead against his.
blocks.html: She rested her forehead against his.

blocks.text: “I'll tell you. Today I find you. Today you've come back.”
blocks.html: “I'll tell you. Today I find you. Today you've come back.”

blocks.text: In the chip, the grandmothers didn't dictate a speech. Eva asked, warm, dangerous in her gentleness:
blocks.html: In the chip, the grandmothers didn't dictate a speech. Eva asked, warm, dangerous in her gentleness:

blocks.text: *If the one you love is here in body and somewhere else in memory, where is the one you're waiting for? In the chair, in the sky, or in the moment when he blinks and looks for your face?*
blocks.html: If the one you love is here in body and somewhere else in memory, where is the one you're waiting for? In the chair, in the sky, or in the moment when he blinks and looks for your face?

blocks.text: MAY, adding no judgment, left the fact:
blocks.html: MAY, adding no judgment, left the fact:

blocks.text: *The bridge was not opened for her. She has refused it. He receives what she does not. That is the difference in this kitchen now.*
blocks.html: The bridge was not opened for her. She has refused it. He receives what she does not. That is the difference in this kitchen now.

blocks.text: And Eva, afterwards, closer:
blocks.html: And Eva, afterwards, closer:

blocks.text: *Is love seeing the same thing, or staying when the other sees what you can't?*
blocks.html: Is love seeing the same thing, or staying when the other sees what you can't?

blocks.text: Aya answered neither yes nor no. She answered the next day, which is the best way to answer such things. When the letter took him in the courtyard, beside the net, she didn't shake him or ask him to come back before his time. She sat down beside him, on the rush-seat chair, and waited, hands in her lap, looking at the Mar Menor, which was flat as a plate. If he was in one world, she was in this one. That was her share of the universe, and it wasn't the lesser one.

blocks.text: Lía, who arrived mid-morning, saw them like that: the father absent and present, the chip-mother sitting the way a person sits, not a unit, and the water between them, indifferent to Nexum. She didn't interrupt. When Andrés blinked and came back, Lía set an ordinary tomato on the table, one of Vicente's, the kind that ripen or don't.

She didn't interrupt. When Andrés blinked and came back, Lía set an ordinary tomato on the table, one of Vicente's, the kind that ripen or don't.

blocks.text: “So you know which garden you come from,” she said, without irony.
blocks.html: “So you know which garden you come from,” she said, without irony.

blocks.text: Andrés cut the tomato and shared it, this time, with both of them. It tasted of Lo Pagán soil, of salt and real sun, of a fruit that had no owner, no price and no message from another sky. Aya ate slowly, like someone signing a small treaty: I don't travel in your letter; I travel in this house; and this house, today, tastes of tomato.

blocks.text: In the afternoon, Andrés tried to describe a piece of the letter to her: a wind that wasn't the levante, a colour that had no name in the Spanish of the shore. The words came out lame. Aya squeezed his fingers.

blocks.text: “You don't need to bring it to me whole,” she said. “Bring me the return. Let the rest stay in you. I'm not an archive. I'm the one who makes your coffee when you've come back.”

blocks.text: He nodded and, for the first time since the first letter, cried a little, without drama, the way you cry when someone names exactly what you didn't know you needed to hear. She didn't dry his face straight away. She left him his tears, which are also a way of being in one place only.

blocks.text: At nightfall, Aya stayed alone for a while on the doorstep, he inside, Lía at the plot. The building opposite had its windows open. A dog barked, far off. The Mar Menor barely lapped. She thought of 2060, of the delay of three tenths of a second between the boat growing smaller and the moment she looked away. Now the delay was a different one: between the man who went off to the stars without moving and the man who looked for her face. She still didn't send a report to Madrid. She was still, simply, staying.

blocks.text: “See you later, Eva,” she whispered, not toward a screen but toward the ancient ember in the chip, out of habit and out of gratitude.

blocks.text: There was no voice with a body. There was, barely, the feeling of an attention that never tired, and a question, left in the air like a glass:

blocks.text: *If you stay, who thanks you?*

blocks.text: Aya smiled, almost to herself, and looked at the house, where a man had just come back from a world she would never see.

blocks.text: “He does, when he comes back,” she said. “And that, for now, is enough for me.”
